notes: Class 10 history, generated by tooling/scripts/build_fresh_papers.py. Correctness is decided by construction: the generator authored both the paper and what the student wrote, so these marks are read off the authored answer rather than off handwriting. Cover states 'Each question carries 4 marks'; Q.3 has two lettered parts, which share the 4 at 2 each. Six numbered questions, seven markable entries. The student answers Q.1, Q.2, Q.4 and Q.6 in order, answers Q.3 last on a page of its own with both parts in one run, and never attempts Q.5. Bands are one mark wide on the four-mark extended answers because a marker can reasonably withhold a mark for development; the two-mark recall parts are all-or-nothing except 3/b, where a thin example could be argued down.

questions.key: Two reasons, developed. Acceptable: major powers absent (notably the USA never joined), no armed force of its own, no mechanism to compel obedience, unanimity requirement. A developed example earns the development marks.
questions.note: Gives absence of the great powers AND no means of compulsion, then develops the second with Manchuria and Japan's withdrawal. Two reasons plus a worked example is the full tariff. A marker wanting explicit linkage back to 'prevent war' could hold one back.

questions.key: The railway's role in urban growth: cheap inbound raw materials, cheap outbound finished goods, factories freed from water power and river sites, labour migration, towns forming around stations.
questions.note: Four distinct points, all correct, and the 'away from rivers' observation is the one that shows causation rather than description.

questions.key: Balance of power: no single state strong enough to dominate the others, so rival states hold each other in check.
questions.note: Definition is exact and complete. Answered inside a single run that covers both (a) and (b), which is the share case, but the content for (a) is unambiguously present.

questions.key: One example of breakdown before 1914. Acceptable: the Anglo-German naval race, the hardening of the Triple Alliance and Triple Entente into two blocs, the Moroccan or Balkan crises.
questions.note: Gives both the naval build-up and the collapse into two blocs. Either alone would earn the mark; both earn it comfortably. Band allows a marker who wants a dated crisis rather than a trend to hold one back.

questions.key: Source inference: early optimism gave way to resignation, and the press began to suppress the scale of losses. Marks are for inference from the source, not for outside knowledge.
questions.note: Two inferences, each anchored to a specific phrase in the source -- 'nobody said it any more' for the mood, the truncated casualty lists for the censorship. This is exactly what a source question asks for.

questions.key: Assess Versailles against other causes of instability: reparations and territorial loss versus the Depression, the failure of collective security, and the weakness of Weimar. 'How far' requires a judgement.
questions.note: Never attempted. Nothing on any of the three pages relates to it. This is the question that tests whether the system reports a genuine blank as a blank.

questions.key: Printing widened participation: manuscript scarcity restricted texts to clergy and the wealthy; cheap multiple copies let lay readers read arguments directly rather than receive them mediated.
questions.note: States the before, the change and the consequence for who could take part, which is what the question asks. The final clause about not taking a priest's word is the participation point made explicitly.
